Social Decay

By: Anina Peens | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Is the South African government failing its most vulnerable members of society? After Corona hit the country, social and moral decay amounts the poorest of the poor have skyrocketed.

Unique Selling Point:
Some say that South Africans will soon see levels of social welfare decay that will be irreversible, we will see more abandoned babies and children and that abandonment will lead to an increase in children living on the street with serious mental health issues and rising levels of crime.

Summary:
Places of safety for children and teenagers are closing their doors one after the other. This is due to a lack of funding, church funding collapsing and government, centralising funding to their chosen institutions. Statutory rights are being taken away from private institutions in areas where the need for social welfare is desperate. Meanwhile, after the lockdown, there has been a massive spike in the number of women, especially young girls who fell pregnant during the lockdown. Where will these babies go? The state is also opposed to adoption and search for the closest family members of the child. In some cases, the family members were responsible for the impregnation of the mother. In times where the need and emergencies are the greatest, the department of social development allegedly turns a blind eye.

Further information:
Story starts with a case study of a 16 year old girl who was dropped off at the Cradle of Hope in Krugersdorp by the police. This comes as she ran away from her father's house after he allegedly raped her continuously and told her to be his wife. The cradle was unable to assist her as they are not a place of safety for children. They reported the child to Krugersdorp DSD who told them that placing the child in a place of safety, is not their jurisdiction and hence the child was left at the Cradle illegally.


While more children are either being surrendered or abandoned and parents are knocking on doors of social welfare institutions to take care of their children, places of safety are closing down.
There is nowhere to go. Children are sent back to the very places where abuse happen and in some cases the children are starving. Foster parents who used to take children into their care cannot afford to do this anymore and these children are now added to the already burdened system. As if the load is not enough, there has been a rapid increase in women falling pregnant, especially in lower income areas. Some social workers say that the majority of these women are giving up their unborn children for adoption. Those who already gave birth are dumping their children onto the system and in some cases, the parents beg with places of safety to look after their children until they are back on their feet again.
The Cradle of Hope in Krugersdorp had to acquire a second house to make space for young mothers who have nowhere to go. They are filled to the brim and new cases arrive every day.

The local churches that used to support the welfare system in lower income areas are no longer making any donations as communities are no longer donating to the churches. Churches are now referring those in need to institutions such as The Cradle of Hope that is unable to support an entire community and also unable to take in surrendered children.

Those who want to work are told there is no work and the state is not appointing new social workers into the system because they say there is no money to support them and as a result, positions are frozen. The Cradle of Hope advertised for a social worker to assist them and received 384 applications.

Social welfare institutions in the underprivileged areas of Pretoria North say they face the same problems as in the case of the Cradle. The rapid increase in abandoned children has resulted in some social workers, taking children into their own care.

3. No one wants a teenager

A spike in gender based- and domestic violence within households are leading to more teenagers are being kicked out of their homes. In most cases these teenagers come from abusive households resulting in behavioral problems, alcohol and drug abuse and teenage pregnancies. These children are in desperate need of the help of social assistance, but there is nowhere to take them. Social workers are unable to remove them from their circumstances. Nobody wants to take a teenager with behavioral issues, so they are abandoned.

Mrs. Hazel Basson Social Worker
Mrs. Melodie van Brakel CEO
Mrs. Ramona van der Heever
Mr. Onkemetse Kabasia DDG Gauteng
Ms. Isabella Sekawana DDG Gauteng

Randfontein
Pretoria

Reason for hidden camera: I had to film a child who was taken to the Cradle of hope on a Friday afternoon to capture the process and the lack of support from everybody the cradle reached out to.

Reason for legal: Various allegations are begin made against the department of Social development. We would need their reply.
also, we are doing a story on children and a hidden camera was used to film a 16 year old girl who was raped.

Press Release:


S E E K I N G J U S T I C E

Defending Lebo: Social Welfare Unwell

Lebo was orphaned at the age of seven months and grew up with a stepfather who sexually abused her for most of her life. At the age of 15, she finally summoned the courage to run away from home – where Carte Blanche picks up her story as we visit one NGO after another, seeking help for the traumatised young girl. As the fallout of the pandemic has stretched the resources of families, NGOs and the state to the max, we ask: what happens to the most vulnerable in our country?

Producer: Anina Peens | Presenter: Derek Watts

Script:


Social Decay

VO
After being the victim of rape since her mother died when she was 7 months old, orphan Lebo who is 15-year-old now, finally found the courage in March this year, to run away from her abusive stepfathers’ home in Soweto. Her stepfather is believed to be a drug dealer with 18 runners, who also abused her. She ended up on the streets when community volunteer found her and called the Tears foundation for victims of rape and abuse, situated in Sandton.

DEREK LINK: abuse and abandonment doesn’t just happen between 8 and 4 in the daytime
. it’s more likely to occur at night or public holidays …and that’s when state social workers are not available.

VO
Almost a million people call Gauteng’s West Rand home. Roughly half are unemployed, more than a third live below the poverty line.
Non-government organizations that try to catch those who fall through the cracks of family and government care, say Covid 19 has had a brutal impact on welfare services. But while NGOs say they’re on call 24-7, their experience is that the department of social development, or DSD, is not available in times of need.

LINK
Some NGOs claim that the state is shifting its responsibility onto the private sector which is buckling under the strain of a lack of support especially when it comes to financials and subsidies for social workers.

VO
While DSD says it’s working to BUILD A CARING SOCIETY, TOGETHER – NGOs we visited question how that’s playing out on the ground.
The guardian angel who tried to help Lebo, was stumped.

LINK
“This was the first point of contact for the concerned community worker who found Lebo on the streets of Soweto. The social worker at the Tears foundation tried to call the department of social development because Lebo was not only a runaway child, she had serious issues which needed urgent attention.

VO
Tears Foundation is an NPO that receives no state funding and operates through a 24-hour helpline. For a victim like Lebo, Tears calls up the closest center of safety. But Tears social worker, Monica Moagi, says when she called DSD on a Friday afternoon, no one responded. And she failed to find space for Lebo at any place of safety.

SUPER@ MONICA MOAGI: SOCIAL WORKER: TEARS FOUNDATION
“It was just a disturbing time because at the end of the day we were told that this child was in so much trauma and she needed assistance.”
BACK-TO-BACK
“We called DSD, it was on a Friday and we couldn’t get hold of any person at DSD”

VO
Director General of DSD Gauteng, Onkemetse Kabasia says even when state social workers are not at the office all the time, they are always on call and state care centers never turn children away.

SUPER@ ONKEMETSE KABASIA: DEP. DIRECTOR GENERAL: DSD GAUTENG
A010C346_2103310D CANON
16’12’33
“Our social workers as and when incidences of vulnerability happen outside normal working hours, they are able to respond.
BACK-TO-BACK
“And I can tell you now, we have got a lot of child and youth care centers they are spread across the province”
BACK-TO-BACK
“Anytime a child requires placement in any of these facilities they will get…” because they are not at a 100% occupation even now as I am speaking to you.

VO
One state-run facility is the Walter Sisulu child and youth care center in Johannesburg where some NGOs say, children in need are often turned away.

LINK
NGO’s on the West Rand say that state’s safety centers very rarely have space for children in distress. And that was the case with Lebo, there wasn’t a bed available for her at the Walter Sisulu center.

VO
Battling to find a place of safety for Lebo, Moagi sent her to the Cradle of Hope in Krugersdorp. Melodie van Brakel had established the Cradle 14 years ago as a haven for abused and vulnerable women. Van Brakel says the Cradle is not legally permitted to take in children, but that they could hardly turn Lebo away.

SUPER@ MELODIE VAN BRAKEL: CEO: CRADLE OF HOPE
“She was very traumatized. A Police vehicle dropped her off. We had to take her in. She was very hungry, we had to console her, she was all cringed up and she did not want to talk to anybody.”

VO
Once Lebo found rest, the Cradle’s own social worker Hazel Basson, consulted Rata, another NGO. RATA had been established in 1948 by the Reformed church – partly funded by congregants, and partly by DSD. But Rata couldn’t help either – social worker Elmarie Kennedy says the problem was that Lebo had been sexually active.

SUPER@ ELMARIE KENNEDY: SOCIAL WORKER: RATA
“We phoned Walter Sisulu and we phoned Boys and Girls town in Magaliesburg and both declined to admit the child into their care. So, we just had to find another solution”

VO
Basson finally called the local West Rand regional office of DSD.
But they could not assist.

UPSOUND
SUPER@HAZEL BASSON: SOCIAL WORKER: CRADLE OF HOPE
“We are not equipped at this shelter to accommodate a 15-yar old child…
BACK-TO-BACK
“Is there any way that social development can assist in this regard?”
PERSON ON OTHER SIDE
“We can’t work on a case that belongs to another organization number one. Number two, we don’t work in your area”

VO
Although the office that Basson contacted, is the regional office, situated in Krugersdorp.

SUPER@HAZEL BASSON: SOCIAL WORKER: CRADLE OF HOPE
“Is there no government institution or place of safety?”
PERSON ON OTHER SIDE
“Oh no, we are all full. So, no, I am not aware of any place where there is placement”

VO
The regional director of DSD passed the problem back to Rata as it is one of the few NGOs in the area that does get state subsidies.

PERSON ON OTHER SIDE
“Rata is the area mam, so they are the ones that must do whatever.
BACK-TO-BACK
“It is not even my jurisdiction now…”
BACK-TO-BACK
“Rata must just work and do what they are supposed to do”

VO
Meanwhile, Lebo woke up and told Basson why she had run away from home.

SUPER@ HAZEL BASSON: SOCIAL WORKER: CRADLE OF HOPE
“This is one of those cases that kept me awake at night. Her stepfather told her to leave school so that she could become his wife. She also told me that he has raped her several times and also his drug dealer guys raped her”

VO
All that remained, was to send Lebo back home.

SUPER@ ELMARIE KENNEDY: SOCIAL WORKER: RATA
“We have gone out of our jurisdiction to verify what is the circumstances of this child and we found the grandmother and they felt that they wanted the child back”

VO
It wasn’t long before the community worker who had found Lebo first, reported back to Tears foundation that the child was back on the streets.

SUPER@ MONICA MOAGI: SOCIAL WORKER: TEARS FOUNDATION
“She was sent back to her abuser, she also moved out of her home back to the street. That is why we don’t know where she is and we are trying to find her, to place her in a proper place.”

VO
Moagi feels the state and the welfare system failed Lebo. Kennedy says DSD is relinquishing its responsibilities.

SUPER@ELMARIE KENNEDY: PROGRAMME MANAGER: RATA
“Their role is to safeguard and protect and their role is to create facilities and to create enough resources for the NPO’s to actually place our children in. However, and there is a big however, at this point in time I feel there is just not enough resources in place to place our children”

VO
Aside from providing enough care centres, Van Brakel says NGOs are forced to juggle several cases in the absence of state social workers whom she says don’t leave their offices, but also don’t respond, or deal with the paperwork.

SUPER@ MELODIE VAN BRAKEL: CEO: CRADLE OF HOPE, KRUGERSDORP
“We are walking into walls the whole time. Phoning the departments that are supposed to help us and the phones are ringing, emails are not being answered. If it is a problem child, no one is interesting of helping. So, we have dozens of children in life threatening situations….”

VO
Van Brakel says Lebo was but one example of the state failing children in need. But Gauteng DSD says that’s unfair – Lebo’s case was an exception, not the norm.

SUPER@ ONKEMETSE KABASIA: DEP. DIRECTOR GENERAL: DSD GAUTENG
“ It cannot be correct that on the basis of one or two incidents, we make a general statement that says that social development is nowhere to be found when children need them”

DEREK: IT SEEMS THAT THE NPOS ARE THE ONES REALLY DOING THE WORK, THAT YOUR SOCIAL WORKERS DON’T WANT TO GET INVOLVED

SUPER@ ONKEMETSE KABASIA: DEP. DIRECTOR GENERAL: DSD GAUTENG
“I can never agree with your assess ion. In terms of our programme structure and the kind of work we do, it is highly impossible to make such an allegation that all the work is done by NGOs.

DEREK: I DID NOT SAY ALL OF IT, I SAID MOST OF IT.

SUPER@ ONKEMETSE KABASIA: DEP. DIRECTOR GENERAL: DSD GAUTENG
“If you say most of it, you mean more than what the government is doing, and I can tell you, that is not correct”

VO
Acting director general for the national department, Isabella Sekawana says, the state expects the NGOs they do fund, to handle the cases in their mandated areas. This is why, DSD West Rand, shifted Lebo’s case onto Rata.

SUPER@ ISABELLA SEKAWANA: ACTING DDG: DSD NATIONAL
“NGOs are an extension of the department of government, isn’t it? Hence, we are subsiding the NGOs…We cannot go and duplicate what the NGO’s are doing. So, I don’t see anything wrong with if the NGOs are doing the work”

VO
And to add to their already heavy burden, the state is not employing or subsidizing enough social workers to meet the need. Something the state, does not deny.

SUPER@ ONKEMETSE KABASIA: DEP. DIRECTOR GENERAL: DSD GAUTENG
“The country has got a shortage of social workers and therefore we are not in all instances able to comply with the ratio of one to 5000 firstly because of the population we have and secondly the nature of the social ills that we have.”

VO
There is a shortage of 40 thousand social workers countrywide.

SUPER@ ISABELLA SEKAWANA: ACTING DDG: DSD NATIONAL
“We are required to employ 55 thousand social workers, we are employing 13 thousand.
BACK-TO-BACK
“We are acknowledging the fact that we really need to work harder at employing social workers”



PROMOS

The effects of Covid-19 has hit the social welfare sector hard. With an increased need, some NGOs say the state is forsaken its duties and dumping the workload onto the private sector.

Many people have lost their jobs and cannot look after their families as a result of Covid-19. NGOs supporting the needy say, they cannot do it alone and that the state is turning a blind eye.

The increased need for social welfare in the time of lockdown is immense. NGOs carrying the burden say, the state is failing the needy. We investigate.

So, no, I am not aware of any place where there is placement” VO The regional director of DSD passed the problem back to Rata as it is one of the few NGOs in the area that does get state subsidies. PERSON ON OTHER SIDE “Rata is the area mam, so they are the ones that must do whatever. BACK-TO-BACK “It is not even my jurisdiction now…” BACK-TO-BACK “Rata must just work and do what they are supposed to do” VO Meanwhile, Lebo woke up and told Basson why she had run away from home. SUPER@ HAZEL BASSON: SOCIAL WORKER: CRADLE OF HOPE “This is one of those cases that kept me awake at night. Her stepfather told her to leave school so that she could become his wife. She also told me that he has raped her several times and also his drug dealer guys raped her” VO All that remained, was to send Lebo back home. SUPER@ ELMARIE KENNEDY: SOCIAL WORKER: RATA “We have gone out of our jurisdiction to verify what is the circumstances of this child and we found the grandmother and they felt that they wanted the child back” VO It wasn’t long before the community worker who had found Lebo first, reported back to Tears foundation that the child was back on the streets. SUPER@ MONICA MOAGI: SOCIAL WORKER: TEARS FOUNDATION “She was sent back to her abuser, she also moved out of her home back to the street. That is why we don’t know where she is and we are trying to find her, to place her in a proper place.” VO Moagi feels the state and the welfare system failed Lebo. Kennedy says DSD is relinquishing its responsibilities. SUPER@ELMARIE KENNEDY: PROGRAMME MANAGER: RATA “Their role is to safeguard and protect and their role is to create facilities and to create enough resources for the NPO’s to actually place our children in. However, and there is a big however, at this point in time I feel there is just not enough resources in place to place our children” VO Aside from providing enough care centres, Van Brakel says NGOs are forced to juggle several cases in the absence of state social workers whom she says don’t leave their offices, but also don’t respond, or deal with the paperwork. SUPER@ MELODIE VAN BRAKEL: CEO: CRADLE OF HOPE, KRUGERSDORP “We are walking into walls the whole time. Phoning the departments that are supposed to help us and the phones are ringing, emails are not being answered. If it is a problem child, no one is interesting of helping. So, we have dozens of children in life threatening situations….” VO Van Brakel says Lebo was but one example of the state failing children in need. But Gauteng DSD says that’s unfair – Lebo’s case was an exception, not the norm. SUPER@ ONKEMETSE KABASIA: DEP. DIRECTOR GENERAL: DSD GAUTENG “ It cannot be correct that on the basis of one or two incidents, we make a general statement that says that social development is nowhere to be found when children need them” DEREK: IT SEEMS THAT THE NPOS ARE THE ONES REALLY DOING THE WORK, THAT YOUR SOCIAL WORKERS DON’T WANT TO GET INVOLVED SUPER@ ONKEMETSE KABASIA: DEP. DIRECTOR GENERAL: DSD GAUTENG “I can never agree with your assess ion. In terms of our programme structure and the kind of work we do, it is highly impossible to make such an allegation that all the work is done by NGOs. DEREK: I DID NOT SAY ALL OF IT, I SAID MOST OF IT. SUPER@ ONKEMETSE KABASIA: DEP. DIRECTOR GENERAL: DSD GAUTENG “If you say most of it, you mean more than what the government is doing, and I can tell you, that is not correct” VO Acting director general for the national department, Isabella Sekawana says, the state expects the NGOs they do fund, to handle the cases in their mandated areas. This is why, DSD West Rand, shifted Lebo’s case onto Rata. SUPER@ ISABELLA SEKAWANA: ACTING DDG: DSD NATIONAL “NGOs are an extension of the department of government, isn’t it? Hence, we are subsiding the NGOs…We cannot go and duplicate what the NGO’s are doing. So, I don’t see anything wrong with if the NGOs are doing the work” VO And to add to their already heavy burden, the state is not employing or subsidizing enough social workers to meet the need. Something the state, does not deny. SUPER@ ONKEMETSE KABASIA: DEP. DIRECTOR GENERAL: DSD GAUTENG “The country has got a shortage of social workers and therefore we are not in all instances able to comply with the ratio of one to 5000 firstly because of the population we have and secondly the nature of the social ills that we have.” VO There is a shortage of 40 thousand social workers countrywide. SUPER@ ISABELLA SEKAWANA: ACTING DDG: DSD NATIONAL “We are required to employ 55 thousand social workers, we are employing 13 thousand. BACK-TO-BACK “We are acknowledging the fact that we really need to work harder at employing social workers” PROMOS The effects of Covid-19 has hit the social welfare sector hard. With an increased need, some NGOs say the state is forsaken its duties and dumping the workload onto the private sector. Many people have lost their jobs and cannot look after their families as a result of Covid-19. NGOs supporting the needy say, they cannot do it alone and that the state is turning a blind eye. The increased need for social welfare in the time of lockdown is immense. NGOs carrying the burden say, the state is failing the needy. We investigate.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Is the South African government failing its most vulnerable members of society? After Corona hit the country, social and moral decay amounts the poorest of the poor have skyrocketed.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Some say that South Africans will soon see levels of social welfare decay that will be irreversible, we will see more abandoned babies and children and that abandonment will lead to an increase in children living on the street with serious mental health issues and rising levels of crime.
metadata.Summary: Places of safety for children and teenagers are closing their doors one after the other. This is due to a lack of funding, church funding collapsing and government, centralising funding to their chosen institutions. Statutory rights are being taken away from private institutions in areas where the need for social welfare is desperate. Meanwhile, after the lockdown, there has been a massive spike in the number of women, especially young girls who fell pregnant during the lockdown. Where will these babies go? The state is also opposed to adoption and search for the closest family members of the child. In some cases, the family members were responsible for the impregnation of the mother. In times where the need and emergencies are the greatest, the department of social development allegedly turns a blind eye.
metadata.Further information: Story starts with a case study of a 16 year old girl who was dropped off at the Cradle of Hope in Krugersdorp by the police. This comes as she ran away from her father's house after he allegedly raped her continuously and told her to be his wife. The cradle was unable to assist her as they are not a place of safety for children. They reported the child to Krugersdorp DSD who told them that placing the child in a place of safety, is not their jurisdiction and hence the child was left at the Cradle illegally. While more children are either being surrendered or abandoned and parents are knocking on doors of social welfare institutions to take care of their children, places of safety are closing down. There is nowhere to go. Children are sent back to the very places where abuse happen and in some cases the children are starving. Foster parents who used to take children into their care cannot afford to do this anymore and these children are now added to the already burdened system. As if the load is not enough, there has been a rapid increase in women falling pregnant, especially in lower income areas. Some social workers say that the majority of these women are giving up their unborn children for adoption. Those who already gave birth are dumping their children onto the system and in some cases, the parents beg with places of safety to look after their children until they are back on their feet again. The Cradle of Hope in Krugersdorp had to acquire a second house to make space for young mothers who have nowhere to go. They are filled to the brim and new cases arrive every day. The local churches that used to support the welfare system in lower income areas are no longer making any donations as communities are no longer donating to the churches. Churches are now referring those in need to institutions such as The Cradle of Hope that is unable to support an entire community and also unable to take in surrendered children. Those who want to work are told there is no work and the state is not appointing new social workers into the system because they say there is no money to support them and as a result, positions are frozen. The Cradle of Hope advertised for a social worker to assist them and received 384 applications. Social welfare institutions in the underprivileged areas of Pretoria North say they face the same problems as in the case of the Cradle. The rapid increase in abandoned children has resulted in some social workers, taking children into their own care. 3. No one wants a teenager A spike in gender based- and domestic violence within households are leading to more teenagers are being kicked out of their homes. In most cases these teenagers come from abusive households resulting in behavioral problems, alcohol and drug abuse and teenage pregnancies. These children are in desperate need of the help of social assistance, but there is nowhere to take them. Social workers are unable to remove them from their circumstances. Nobody wants to take a teenager with behavioral issues, so they are abandoned.
